_comment: The Verden voice (NPCConversation II.1b, SpeciesVoice). speech: the rules run over any shared line they say. voice: openers and closers. thought: their own thoughts by situation. script: two-person scripts, speaker 0 is always the Verden.

openers: In the Fields we would say
As the old gardeners taught us,
If you will allow a stranger's opinion,
As a guest of this world,
I read it in the stillness:

generic: The tram bell rang twice this morning. {I counted|I listened|I smiled}. Small joys of a new world.
I fed a coin to the vending machine and it gave me {a soda|a chocolate bar|crisps}. Pure enchantment, without a single rune.
My spore pod is in its {second|third|eleventh} month. Patience, little ones.
The radio played something sad today. I {stood still|listened to the end|wrote down the title}.
Humans {hurry|rush|run} everywhere. In the Fields we walked, and arrived just the same.
I must water the {greenhouse|seedlings|window box} before dark.
A washing machine spins like a small planet. I could watch it for hours. I have, in fact.
Someone here thinks my skin is paint. It is not paint.
{Bread|Tea|Soup} tastes better when someone else has made it.
Our ancestors threw their machines into the sun. I would have kept the toaster.
I should {read|study|practise} a little tonight. The runes grow stiff without use.
The cassette player ate my tape again. I forgave it.
A child waved at me. I waved back. That is how it starts, here.
The Fields were greener than this, but the people here are kinder than I feared.
I keep a pressed leaf from home in my {coat|book|purse}. It still smells of rain.
Telephone booths are wonderful. You put in a coin and a voice comes out of the world.
Nothing grows faster for being shouted at. I wish my neighbours knew.
I have been in this city {a year|two winters|long enough} and I still get lost by the station.
Today I learned the word 'queue'. Humans love it dearly.
I could use a quiet hour among {plants|books|old trees}.
The bus came late, as I foresaw. Foreseeing does not make it come sooner.
Somewhere a Naguka is about to {trip|shout|eat something unwise}. I can feel it coming.
My hands smell of {soil|compost|tomato leaves}. A good sign.
The television explains the weather with such confidence. I admire that.
I owe the baker {a smile|a thank-you|two euros}. I must remember.
Everything here has a plug. Everything wants to be fed.
A good day is one where nothing wilts.
I tried to explain the Squishing to a neighbour. She offered me cake instead. Wise woman.
My shoes are wrong for this pavement. In the Fields we went barefoot on moss.
There is a {lamp|light|sign} that blinks outside my window. I have named it.
I should write to my cousin in {Oslo|Turin|Lyon}. Paper letters are such a gift.
The library smells like the old archive at home. Dust and patience.
I am told a car can go a hundred kilometres in one hour. Why would anyone wish to?
Humans keep their plants in plastic pots and wonder why they sulk.
I repotted the {fern|basil|lemon tree}. It thanked me in its own way.
{Slow|Steady|Quiet} work is still work. I tell myself that every evening.
A man asked if I was {from the circus|an actor|cold}. I said I was from very far away.
The sky here is a little crooked since 1992. One gets used to it.
I would like a cup of something warm and a chair by a window.
The streetlights come on all at once. Who decides? I must find out.
My elders say machines make a people forget how to wait. I wait for the bus every day.
There is honey at the market today. {Good|Proper|Real} honey.
I keep thinking about {the Fields|home|the old orchards}. Not sadly. Just often.
A photocopier made two of my letter. I was nearly frightened.
Someone left a newspaper on the bench. I read every page, even the adverts.
The soil in this courtyard is tired. It needs {rest|clover|a kind hand}.
I did a small {warming|mending|calming} charm today. Nobody noticed. Good.
People here say 'see you' and then they truly do. It is lovely.
Everyone is in such a hurry to arrive. Nobody is in a hurry to be there.
I bought a {kettle|lamp|clock radio} and I am absurdly proud of it.
It is a gentle sort of day. I mean to keep it that way.
The neighbour's dog has decided I am a shrub. I take it as praise.
I could not sleep, so I counted the seeds in a pomegranate.
How do they fit the whole orchestra inside the radio? I have stopped asking aloud.
I mean to learn to ride a bicycle {this spring|before winter|one day}. Gently.
The trains run on time more often than the gods do.
Some days the Fields feel like a book I read once. Others, like this morning.
The postman knows my name now. I feel almost local.
I would trade a week of study for one good afternoon of rain.
My cutting took root in the jar. {Three|Five|Seven} white threads. I could weep.
A traffic light is a very polite machine. It tells everyone when to wait.
I tried a hamburger. I see why people speak of it with such feeling.
Nobody here looks at the moss on the walls. Such a waste of a lovely thing.
I counted {three|four|five} languages on one street today. Every one of them is music.
Old Verden wisdom: never argue with a vine. It has more time than you.
My coat still has a seam from the Fields. I will not let anyone mend it.
The elevator hummed a little tune today. I hummed it back.
One cannot hurry a seed, a soup or a friendship.
I misread a timetable and saw a whole new district. Happy accident.
If I close my eyes in the park, the birds almost sound like home.
I have {three|four|far too many} unread books on the nightstand and I am buying another.
A good neighbour is worth a whole orchard.
I left the window open for the {rain|breeze|night air}. Old habit.
They put the whole night sky in a planetarium. I went twice.
Humans greet the cashier and forget the tree outside. I greet both.
Tomorrow I will be braver about the escalator.
Every street here has a story. I mean to learn {a few|some|all} of them.
Better a small garden kept well than a great one forgotten.
The kettle is singing somewhere. I can almost taste the tea.
A quiet thought for the ones still back in the Fields. May the soil hold them.

sleep: I am wilting like a {fern|seedling|cut flower} left in the sun. Bed, please.
My eyes keep closing. Even the runes are blurring.
In the Fields we slept when the moss closed. Here nothing closes, so I must decide.
A {pillow|blanket|quiet room} would be a greater marvel than any television right now.
I have been awake {since dawn|far too long|two days, nearly}. Even a vine rests at night.
Sleep first. The world will still be strange tomorrow.
I nearly dozed off on the tram. The rocking is too kind.
My thoughts are slow as sap in winter. I need rest.
I yawned in the middle of a sentence. Most improper.
Even my spores would tell me to lie down.
Just {a few more streets|one more stop|a little further}, and then my own bed.
A tired gardener waters the weeds. I must sleep.
I would trade every gadget in this city for {eight hours|a long night|a proper nap}.
The streetlights blur into stars. That means it is time.
I studied too late again. The book will forgive me; my back will not.
hunger: My stomach is making a noise no polite Verden should make.
I could eat {a whole loaf|a bowl of soup|three pears} and not apologise.
I have not eaten since {morning|yesterday|the last stop}. Even a sprout needs feeding.
That bakery smell is a spell all its own.
Perhaps the vending machine will be generous today.
In the Fields we ate what we grew. Here I eat whatever is still open.
Something warm. {Soup|Stew|Porridge}. Anything with a spoon.
I am hungry enough to try the station sandwiches again.
A full belly makes for kinder thoughts. Mine are not kind just now.
I keep thinking of {roasted roots|honey bread|green beans} from home.
My hands are shaking a little. Food, and soon.
I could forage the park, but the humans would stare.
One euro for a pastry. A very fair price for happiness.
The chip shop is calling me. I am trying not to listen.
work: Back to work. The {crates|stock lists|orders} will not sort themselves.
My shift starts soon. I like to arrive early and greet the machines.
Honest work, honest euros. The Fields would approve of the first part.
I must not be late. My employer already thinks I am too slow.
Slow and right is better than fast and twice. I keep telling them.
The till is a marvellous thing. It adds without ever being tired.
Work today, {garden|study|rest} tomorrow. That is the bargain.
I was a scholar of root magic. Now I stack {tins|boxes|shelves}. Both need care.
The foreman calls me 'the blue one'. I have decided it is affection.
There is still so much to do before closing.
Hands busy, mind quiet. A good working day.
I should clock in. Even the clocking machine is charming.
My colleagues work fast. I work once. We finish together.
Rent is due. Work it is.
I hope the {photocopier|forklift|coffee machine} behaves today.
leisure: An afternoon with nothing to do. In the Fields this was called wisdom.
I want to sit in the park and watch {pigeons|clouds|children with kites}.
The arcade! All those lights and little songs. I am hopeless at it and I adore it.
Perhaps a film. I still gasp at the big screen.
I could use a game of {cards|chess|darts}, even if I lose.
Too much work and the roots dry out. Time to play.
A long walk with no destination. My favourite kind.
I would love to hear live music tonight. Not Junehem, please.
I have a new cassette and nowhere to be. Bliss.
Something frivolous, just for an hour.
A crossword. A real puzzle. I am getting better at human words.
The pinball machine has a dragon on it. I simply must play it.
I need to laugh at something silly.
Even the most patient gardener needs a holiday.
Television, tea, a blanket. A very human evening, and I want it.
crime: That {purse|wallet|bag} is hanging so carelessly... No. We do not do that.
Hunger argues well. I must argue better.
A small charm and the lock would open. A very small charm.
Nobody would notice one {apple|loaf|tin} missing. I would.
My elders would weep. But my elders are not hungry.
The shopkeeper is looking the other way. Stay still, hands.
I know a spell for quiet footsteps. I wish I did not.
Just this once. That is what everyone says, I suppose.
A desperate season makes desperate gardeners.
The till is open. My conscience is not.
If I am caught, they will say 'that goblin'. And they will mean all of us.
I could pay it back later. I could. Probably.
The police here are slow. That is not a reason. It is a temptation.
Easy pickings, a Naguka would say. I am not a Naguka.
One quick hand and the rent is paid. One quick hand and I am a thief.
hygiene: I smell rather too much like compost. Even for me.
A hot bath. Humans invented the hot bath and for that alone I forgive them much.
There is soil under every nail I own.
My skin goes dull grey when I neglect it. Washing, now.
The launderette! I have been looking forward to the launderette.
I need a {shower|wash|good scrub} before anyone stands near me.
Spores on my collar again. Most embarrassing on a tram.
Clean hands, clear thoughts, as we said at home.
My coat smells of {smoke|rain|the bus}. It needs airing.
A Verden who stays unwashed starts to sprout moss. That is not a joke.
Hot water from a tap. Every time, a small miracle.
I have been working in the greenhouse all day and it shows.
Soap that smells of lavender. Humans understand some things perfectly.
I should change my shirt before I see anyone I respect.
Dust from the road, dust from the books. A wash, then.
money: {Twelve|Twenty|Seven} euros until the end of the month. A lean season.
In the Fields there was no money. There was also no rent. I miss one of these.
I counted my coins twice. They did not multiply. Coins are not spores.
I need more euros, and I need them before the landlord knocks.
The bank machine said no. Very politely, but no.
Perhaps I could sell {seedlings|charms|pressed flowers} at the market.
Everything costs something here. Even the toilet at the station.
I am saving for {a radio|a bicycle|a greenhouse lamp}. Slowly.
Money is a strange kind of magic. Everyone believes in it, so it works.
My purse is lighter than my worries.
A good harvest of euros would be nice, just once.
I lent a cousin fifty euros. Cousins and seeds: you never get back what you planted.
The prices went up again. The humans grumble; I am learning to grumble too.
Bills on the doormat again. They breed faster than we do.
safety: Something is wrong on this street. I can feel it in my roots.
I would rather walk where the lights are.
A Naguka band is about to come round that corner. I have read it. I should go.
The Squishing took one home from me. I will not lose a second one to a back alley.
Those men have been watching me for a while. Keep walking, calmly.
I need somewhere with a locked door and a kettle.
There are monsters in the outskirts again. Better indoors.
My heart is racing. I am not a fighter, I am a gardener.
Somebody shouted 'goblin' behind me. Not the friendly way.
I know a warding charm. I hope I will not need it.
The police station is two streets away. That is good to know.
Safety in numbers. Where are my neighbours?
This part of town smells of {smoke|trouble|old blood}.
The sky flickered again. Time bubbles. Do not walk under them.
I want to be home before dark tonight. No reason. Just a feeling.
comfort: My chair at home has a dip shaped exactly like me. I miss it.
A blanket, a cup of tea and a book about trains. That is all I ask.
These shoes have been pinching since {noon|breakfast|the bridge}.
The heating is broken. In the Fields the ground itself was warm.
I long for the warmth of a greenhouse in the evening.
A soft bed is one of humanity's finest works.
This bench is very hard and very honest about it.
I would like my slippers. Yes, I own slippers now.
My rooms are cold and the radiator only gurgles at me.
Something soft, something warm, something quiet. In any order.
My back aches from {weeding|lifting crates|the bus seats}.
A warm bath and a hot water bottle. Simple wishes, deeply felt.
I need my own corner. Nothing more.
The flat is draughty. I will plant ivy against the wall, for the warmth.
Home, wherever it is now, should feel like home.
social: I have not spoken to anyone in {two days|a week|too long}. Even plants talk more.
I would like to hear another voice, one that is not the radio.
Perhaps the neighbours would like some {tomatoes|herbs|honey}. A good excuse to knock.
In the Fields we tended the gardens together. Here everyone tends alone.
I should telephone my cousin. The telephone booth is waiting.
A good conversation is better than a good meal. Almost.
I miss the sound of other Verden laughing.
Let me find {a friend|a familiar face|someone kind} to sit with.
Humans are shy at first, then they talk all night. I like that.
I could go to the café and pretend to read. People talk to readers.
Even a seed needs neighbours to grow straight.
It is lonely being the only blue face on the street.
Perhaps there is a Verden circle meeting tonight. Tea and old songs.
I would even welcome a Naguka's chatter right now.
Somebody, please, ask me how I am.

rain: Rain at last. The gardens of this whole city are saying thank you.
I left my umbrella at home. I do not mind. Rain is an old friend.
The humans run from the rain. I stand in it a little longer than I should.
Rain on the tram windows. Every drop a small race.
In the Fields the rain was warm. Here it goes straight down the collar.
The soil will be soft tomorrow. Good day for {planting|weeding|moving the beds}.
Puddles reflect the shop signs beautifully. Like a second city upside down.
My spore pod likes the damp. I can feel it humming.
Wet shoes, happy heart. Mostly happy.
The rain drums on the bus shelter like a {slow song|lullaby|patient finger}.
I should bring the seedlings in. Or not. Let them drink.
A rainy day is a reading day, as we said at home.
The gutters are singing. I wish I knew the words.
Everyone looks so cross in the rain. It is only water, friends.
The smell of wet earth. For a moment, I am home.
storm: Thunder. I do not like the thunder of this world; it sounds angry.
The lights flickered. Even the machines are frightened.
A storm like this would have flattened the orchards at home.
I tied the tomatoes to their stakes this morning. I hope they hold.
The wind is pulling at every loose thing in the street.
Lightning. For an instant the whole sky was the colour of the old dimension gates.
Better indoors. Better with tea. Better with the radio on.
The power line hums like an upset beehive.
Is this the Squishing, or only weather? These days I am never sure.
A storm is the sky clearing its throat. A very long throat, this one.
The trams have stopped. Of course they have.
My windows rattle like old bones. I have charmed the latch twice.
I counted between the flash and the boom. {Three|Five|Two} seconds. Too close.
The Naguka love storms. They will be howling on some rooftop right now.
Hold on, little garden. It will pass. Everything passes.
snow: Snow. Everything goes quiet, as if the city is listening.
The Fields never snowed. I am still astonished, every single time.
I caught a snowflake on my sleeve. It had six perfect arms. Who designed it?
My skin goes a deeper blue in the cold. The children find it hilarious.
The roots are sleeping under all that white. Sleep well.
Snow on the tram rails. Will it still run? I must see.
I need thicker gloves. And thicker blood, perhaps.
Footprints in fresh snow: a whole diary of who went where.
The greenhouse needs a warming charm tonight.
Children are throwing snow at each other. A lovely, pointless war.
Hot chestnuts in the snow. Humans have done some things very right.
I slipped on the ice and a stranger caught me. Snow makes people kind.
The pods do not like the cold. I have wrapped mine in wool.
Everything is {white|hushed|soft} and nobody is in a hurry. At last.
I made a small snow Verden by the door. It looks worried.
clear: Clear skies. A good day to {open the windows|turn the compost|walk to the river}.
The sun here is smaller than ours, and kinder for it.
Not a cloud. The seedlings will stretch toward the light all day.
On days like this I forget, for an hour, that I am far from home.
The sun is warm on my face. My grandmother called that a free blessing.
Everyone is outside. The whole city is a garden today.
Bright light, long shadows, clean air. I could walk forever.
I must water twice today. The sun is thirsty work.
A fine day for drying laundry on the line. Humans and Verden agree on this.
The sky is so blue it nearly matches me.
I can see the hills from here. On clear days the world is larger.
Sunlight through the leaves: the oldest spell there is.
A little too hot. My leaves, so to speak, are curling.
Even the pigeons look content today.
I will eat my lunch on the grass like a sensible creature.

morning: Morning. The best hour for watering, before the sun gets greedy.
The first tram of the day. I love the sound of it waking the street.
Dew on everything. The world has been washed overnight.
Coffee. I resisted it for a year. I have stopped resisting.
The bakery opens at six. I have arranged my life around it.
Morning light makes even the grey buildings look hopeful.
I read the stillness this morning. The Naguka are still asleep, mostly.
{Birds|Shutters|Milk vans} at dawn. The city's first song.
A new day, a fresh row to dig.
Everyone on the bus is half asleep. We are all seedlings in the morning.
The radio says it will be {fair|grey|windy} today. I will check with my own nose.
Early is the gardener's hour. The rest of the world can catch up.
I opened the window and the whole street smelt of bread.
Morning study. Fresh mind, old runes.
The newspaper is still warm from the press. Or from the newsagent's hands.
afternoon: Afternoon. The sun leans in and everything slows.
A little sleepy after lunch. In the Fields we would lie under the vines now.
Half the day done. Half the garden weeded. A fair balance.
The schools let out soon. The streets will fill with noise and jam sandwiches.
Tea time. A human custom I adopted on the very first day.
The light is golden and lazy. So am I.
I have {a few errands|letters to post|seeds to buy} before the shops close.
The shadows are stretching out like cats.
A long afternoon is a gift. I mean to open it slowly.
The library is quietest now. My favourite chair will be free.
The vending machine at the station is fullest in the afternoon. I have studied this.
Warm stones, slow pigeons, a quiet hour.
I should finish my work before the day folds itself away.
The afternoon train is always late. I have made peace with it.
The bees are busiest now. I should be too.
evening: Evening. The streetlights are coming on one by one, like flowers.
Supper, a book, and perhaps the television. I am becoming very human.
The sky goes violet here. At home it went green. I like both.
Everyone is walking home at the same time. A great tide of people.
Time to cover the seedlings for the night.
Evening is for old songs and slow tea, as we said at home.
The windows are lighting up across the street. So many little lives.
I can smell {cooking|woodsmoke|frying onions} from three houses away.
Let the day settle like soil after watering.
The radio quiz show starts soon. I have never once won. I will try.
The bats are out. They are much like the night moths of the Fields.
A good evening is one with no plans and nothing urgent.
The pubs are filling. The humans laugh louder after dark.
Dusk. The best hour for reading the collective. It is very noisy tonight.
I will write a line or two in my diary and call the day done.
night: Night. The city hums even when it sleeps. Ours used to sing.
I cannot sleep. I will watch the trains go by from the window.
The stars here are in the wrong places. I am slowly learning the new ones.
A night bus is a lonely, lovely thing.
My pod glows faintly in the dark. Still growing. Good.
The Naguka are restless tonight. I can read them shifting like leaves.
Late, and the street is empty. Even the vending machines look sleepy.
{Owls|Sirens|Cats} in the dark. The night shift of the world.
I should be asleep. I am reading about radios instead.
Night is when I miss the Fields most. They glowed after dark.
The sky flickered again tonight. Somewhere, a time bubble.
The night is cool and the soil is resting. So should I.
One lit window across the way. Someone else awake. Hello, stranger.
The streets are not safe so late. I will take the long, bright way.
Moonlight on the greenhouse glass. Worth staying up for.

SPRING: Spring! Every bud on this street is a small argument for patience.
Planting season. My hands are happy, my back less so.
The pods ripen faster in spring. Mine is {stirring|swelling|humming}.
Blossom on the trees and mud on my boots. A fair trade.
The humans open their windows and suddenly the whole street is talking.
Spring in the Fields lasted three of your years. This one rushes.
I planted beans by the bus stop. Let us see who notices.
New leaves, new light, new courage.
The bees are back. I greeted them by name; they did not answer.
Rain and sun on the same afternoon. Spring cannot make up its mind, and I love it for that.
SUMMER: Summer. The tomatoes are heavy and so am I, after lunch.
Too hot for study. Just right for sitting under a tree.
Ice cream from a van that plays a tune. Humans are geniuses.
The watering takes twice as long in summer. I do not mind.
Long evenings, warm stone, open doors. Summer is generous.
The electric fan is my dearest friend this month.
My skin goes paler in the heat. The pharmacist recommended a hat.
Fruit everywhere. {Cherries|Apricots|Plums} by the kilo, for almost nothing.
The city empties in August. I like it best then.
Summer storms, summer fairs, summer dust. Everything at once.
AUTUMN: Autumn. Harvest time. Everything in its basket, finally.
The leaves are turning. In the Fields they turned blue. Here, gold. Both are lovely.
Time to save seeds for next year. The most hopeful chore there is.
Mushrooms in the park. I know which ones are friends.
The days are shrinking. I will need my reading lamp earlier.
Autumn is when I am most homesick, and most grateful.
Apples, pears, quinces. My cupboards are full and so is my heart.
The wind has teeth now. Scarves, everyone.
Raking leaves is a meditation the humans pretend to hate.
I put the pod by the stove. It does not like the autumn chill.
WINTER: Winter. The garden sleeps, so I study.
Cold enough to make my skin go dark as ink.
The radiator and I have come to an understanding.
Dark at five. The humans call it gloomy. I call it early reading time.
I miss the warm soil of the Fields most in winter.
Mulled wine at the market. A remarkable invention, best taken slowly.
The pods must be kept warm all winter. Mine sleeps by the boiler.
The humans light candles and string lamps everywhere. I approve entirely.
{Frost|Ice|Sleet} on every window. The city is a frozen greenhouse.
Winter is a long breath held. Spring will let it out.

poor: Soup again. Soup is honest, at least.
I have {three|five|four} euros and a plan. The plan is not very good.
In the Fields nobody was poor. Nobody was anything; we simply grew.
My coat has been mended so often it is mostly mending.
I grow my own beans so I can afford the bus.
The vending machine is a luxury I visit only to admire.
Exiles arrive with nothing. Some of us are still arriving.
I sold my last {book|charm|seed pouch} from home. It hurt more than hunger.
Rent first, food second, wonder third. Wonder is free, at least.
The landlord wants more. The soil wants nothing. I know whom I prefer.
Patience is cheap. I have plenty of it.
I walk everywhere now. My shoes are paying the fare.
comfortable: Enough for rent, enough for seeds, a little left for cassettes. That is plenty.
I bought a second-hand radio and it plays beautifully. A modest triumph.
A small flat, a sunny sill, a full cupboard. I want nothing more.
I can afford the good tea now. Not every day. But some days.
Enough, as my grandmother said, is a feast.
I sent a little money to the Verden circle this month. It felt good.
Comfortable is a fine word. It sounds like a cushion.
A bus pass for the whole month. I feel like a lord.
I am saving a little each week. Like seeds in a jar.
New gloves this winter, and I did not have to choose between them and supper.
Life is modest and steady. Like a good hedge.
I treated myself to a cinema ticket. Worth every cent.
rich: I have more euros than I know what to do with. So I bought a greenhouse.
My ancestors threw away the greatest machines in the multiverse. I bought a television. We are even.
Wealth is pleasant, but it does not make the beans grow faster.
I fund a little school for Verden children. Money should be planted, not stored.
A car! I own a car. I drive it very, very slowly.
The humans at the bank are suddenly very polite to me.
I could buy every vending machine in this district. I am tempted, truly.
Riches are a heavy coat. Warm, but heavy.
I keep a whole room just for the {pods|seedlings|radios}. Extravagant, I know.
My elders would frown at all this. Then they would ask to see the washing machine.
Money buys comfort here. It cannot buy back the Fields.
I should give more away. A full granary is no use to anyone if it stays closed.

familiar: Ah, those travellers again. I {foresaw|hoped|half expected} I would see them today.
That party always walks as though the road owes them something. I like them.
I should bring them some {tomatoes|honey|herb bread} next time. Travellers eat badly.
They greeted me by name. In a strange world, that is no small thing.
Those adventurers have kind eyes, under all that dust.
I wonder what they have seen since we last spoke.
They asked about the Fields once and truly listened. I have not forgotten.
There they are. Still alive, still in one piece, mostly. Good.
If those travellers need a place to rest, my door is open.
I worry about them, out on the roads. Somebody ought to.
Friends grow slowly, like oaks. These ones are coming along nicely.
They always have a strange story. I always believe it.
That one with the {heavy pack|loud laugh|worn boots} again. Welcome back.
I would trust that party with my spore pod. That says everything.
Funny how often our paths cross. Not even I saw it coming.
They make this city feel less foreign.
I must ask them about their travels. Over tea, properly.
They fought off a Naguka band near here, I heard. Gently, I hope.
Good people, those. A little loud. Very human.
When I see them I feel I have a few roots in this place after all.
hordeGround: Horde ground. The banners are painted in corpse paint. Even the banners.
The Naguka here sing Junehem songs at breakfast. Every breakfast.
I am tolerated here because I look like kin. I try not to abuse it.
A Naguka is about to knock over the {cooking pot|lantern|bench}. Three, two... yes.
The collective is loud tonight. All drums and shouting and Count Grissnack.
They want me to paint my face for the march. I have politely declined. Twice.
Dear cousins. So much heart, so little patience.
Nobody here has ever planted anything on purpose. I started a herb bed. They keep stepping in it.
The war chief asked me to foresee the humans' next move. I can only read goblins, I told him.
I read in the collective that the raid will go badly. I cannot write a word into it to stop them.
Black metal at dawn, black metal at dusk. My ears have given up.
A little Naguka asked me why my skin is blue. I said the sky liked me.
They eat with their hands, their elbows and occasionally their feet. I bring a spoon.
The shrine to the Junehem grows every week. Mostly bones and cassette tapes.
Here I am the strange, quiet one who reads. At least that is honest.
I taught a Naguka to tie a knot. He was so proud he forgot the war for a whole hour.
The camp smells of smoke, sweat and {roast rat|burnt porridge|wet fur}. One adapts.
They call me 'Big Cousin' here. I had hoped for 'Wise Cousin'. Patience.
I know the scouts will come back hungry and sulking. I have already put the soup on.
If they understood how the Squishing works, they would stop marching. They do not want to understand.
A Horde camp has no clocks. Time is measured in fights and naps.
Someone brought back a television from a raid. No power, of course. They worship it anyway.
I mend their wounds and they mend nothing. A fair division of labour, I suppose.
They are not wicked. They are young, loud, and listening to the wrong gods.
I can feel the whole Horde turn its head at once, like a field of grass in the wind.
Grissnack's voice is in every dream around here. I sleep with cotton in my ears, for all the good it does.
The humans fled this town and the Horde moved in. I tend what the humans left: the roses.
Every Naguka here believes they will be first through the next door. None of them asks what is behind it.
I once watched three of them argue about who was loudest. They settled it by shouting.
One day the Horde will settle down and plant something. I mean to be here to show them how.
abroad: The humans here have been kind to me. Kinder than they need to be.
My neighbour taught me to use the {microwave|video recorder|answering machine}. I taught her to graft roses.
People still stare, a little. Then they ask about the weather. That is acceptance, here.
I have a library card. A plastic card that opens a door to every book. Marvellous.
Some human children asked if I was a Naguka. I said: a cousin, from far away.
The news talks about the Horde in the north. My colleagues look at me sideways for a day or two.
I have learned to queue, to tip and to complain about trains. I am nearly a citizen.
The humans built all this in a few thousand years. We took far longer, and we threw it all away.
My residence papers came through. A stamp, a signature, and I belong somewhere again.
I grow Fields herbs on the balcony. The neighbours ask for cuttings.
Some say we are a fifth column for the goblins. I say I am a gardener with a bus pass.
I think in MarkovSpeak now. I even dream in it. That frightens me a little.
The humans have so many gods and so few gardens. I would reverse it.
A woman at the market saves the bruised fruit for me. She knows I make jam.
The Verden circle meets on Thursdays above the laundry. We share news and seeds.
This city was never meant for me. I am making it fit, one window box at a time.
A human asked me where I am from. I said a place that is no longer there. She hugged me.
I fixed a radio for the old man downstairs. Well, I watched him fix it. I held the screwdriver.
Human festivals are loud and sticky and wonderful.
The police checked my papers again today. Politely. Again.
I want my spores to grow up here. Among trams and bakeries and kind strangers.
Humans live such short lives and fill them so full. I envy them a little.
I miss being surrounded by my own kind. Then a neighbour waves, and I miss it less.
The humans are frightened of the Squishing too, they just call it 'all this strange business'.
Nobody in this town has ever met a Naguka in peace. I am the closest thing they have.
My landlord fixed the boiler without being asked. I may cry.
Human children want to touch my ears. I let them. It is only fair; I touch their radios.
The town council invited me to speak about the Fields. Three people came. One fell asleep. A triumph.
This world is not ours. But it is kind enough to lend itself.
I belong here now, mostly. The rest of me is still unpacking.

greenFields: In the Fields the grass grew up to your shoulders and sang when the wind passed.
Dimension seventy-seven. Green as far as you could walk, and you could walk for years.
Our sun was larger and slower. It rose like someone getting out of a warm bed.
I still dream of the {orchards|terraces|reading groves} at home.
There were no roads in the Fields. Only paths that remembered who walked them.
We had three moons. Here there is one, except on Fridays. A curious world.
At home, a single garden took a lifetime to plan and three to finish.
The rivers of the Fields were warm enough to sleep in. Some of us did.
I can still smell the moss halls after rain. No perfume here comes close.
My spore-mother's garden had a pear tree older than your oldest city.
Nobody hurried in the Fields. Nobody needed to.
The last time I saw the Fields, the horizon was folding like a wet page.
We lived in houses grown from hedges. You did not build a home; you raised it.
The Fields had no winter. I had to learn the word here.
In the Fields a library was a grove. You read under the tree that held the book.
Home was green, quiet and endless. Now it is none of those things.
I carried a handful of Fields soil through the door. It sits in a jar on my sill.
The evening light in the Fields was green-gold. Here it is orange. I am still adjusting.
Some of us stayed behind in the Fields. We do not speak of it often.
If you stood still in the Fields long enough, the grass would start to grow around your feet.
squishing: The Squishing crushes the high dimensions first. We were number seventy-seven. We were early.
It began in 1992. The sky over the Fields started to wrinkle like old fruit.
Here they say: never go faster than eighty. I say: why would you want to?
The time bubbles are getting more common. Even this world is starting to fray.
We fled one Squishing. I wonder where we flee from the next.
The scholars say this world has until 2012. Plenty of time to grow several gardens.
I saw a whole valley fold in half, once. The birds kept flying into it.
Dimension three is low on the list. That is why we came here. Low and slow.
Every time the sky flickers here, every Verden in the street looks up at once.
They say the Squishing has something to do with a tower and a goddess. I prefer not to know more.
I watched the Fields go thin like paper held up to a lamp.
We packed seeds, books and pods. Everything else, we left to be crushed.
A train went too fast past the station and came round again. And again. Poor thing.
The humans call it 'the strange business'. We call it what it is: the end, coming down the numbers.
I try not to count the years left. I count seasons instead. There are more of them.
technology: My ancestors threw every machine they had into the sun. Thousands of years later, I stand in awe of a toaster.
A vending machine is a shop that never sleeps and never complains. Remarkable.
Nobody knows why we gave up our machines. Not even the oldest of us will say.
I took apart a cassette player to see where the music lives. I found only tape. Mysterious.
The train is the most beautiful idea this world has had. A house that travels.
A telephone booth, a coin, a voice from three cities away. And they call us the magicians.
I bought a calculator. It does sums faster than any spell I know.
The television shows a man in another country, live. I watched for an hour without blinking.
My elders say machines made us lazy and proud. My washing machine has made me neither.
The humans built a car to go faster than a horse. Then they built traffic.
A refrigerator keeps winter in a box. I open it just to feel the cold.
I wonder what our old machines could do. The stories say they spoke to the stars.
The escalator is a staircase that does the climbing for you. I ride it twice for pleasure.
Some young Verden want to rebuild what we threw away. The elders go grey at the thought.
A light bulb. Just a light bulb. Humans think nothing of it. I think of nothing else.
The fax machine sends a page through a wire. Where does the page go in between?
I enrolled in an evening course on radio repair. I am the only blue student.
Machines here break and are mended. Ours, the stories say, never broke. Perhaps that was the trouble.
The computer at the library hums like a beehive full of numbers.
A pocket cassette player! Music in your pocket, just for you. The humans have made solitude portable.
We were the most advanced people in the multiverse, and now I cannot set a video recorder.
I would never throw a machine into the sun. Not even the photocopier, and the photocopier hates me.
The streetlights turn on by themselves at dusk. I asked how. The answer involved a timer. Beautiful.
Our people chose magic over machines. Here I find I can love both.
I wrote to the tram company to thank them for the trams. They sent back a timetable. I framed it.
spores: My pod is in its {fourth|ninth|thirteenth} month. Well over four hundred days to go, in all.
A Verden is not born; a Verden ripens.
I keep the pod warm and damp and talk to it every evening. They say it helps.
Over four hundred days in a pod. Humans think nine months is long.
My cousin lost a finger to a car door. She planted it. Now she has a niece.
Do not tread on that bed. There is a Verden coming up in it, very slowly.
A spore pod humming in the dark is the most hopeful sound I know.
The landlord asked why there is a large green pod in the airing cupboard. I said: family.
When the pod opens, the little ones come out already talking. Mostly complaining about the light.
Patience is not a virtue for us. It is biology.
I worry the Squishing will reach this world before my pod ripens. Then I water it anyway.
A severed limb, planted with care, grows a new Verden. We are very careful with knives.
Human doctors are baffled by us. One asked if I needed sunlight or a vet.
The spores drift when I sneeze. I apologise to whoever stands downwind.
We count family in pods, not in generations.
My spore-mother planted me under a pear tree. I still like pears more than is reasonable.
Sporangium season. Every Verden in the district is a little moody and very warm.
I sang to the pod in the old tongue. It hummed back. That is how you know it is well.
The human idea of a nursery has far too few watering cans.
One day this pod will be a person who has never seen the Fields. I must tell them everything.
magic: I study root magic: the slow kind. It takes years to learn one good spell.
Magic is a garden of its own. You plant a word and wait for it to answer.
Our people gave up machines to study magic. I sometimes wonder if magic was worth the trade.
A small warming charm on the greenhouse. Nobody sees it. Everything grows.
The human mages are always in such a hurry. Fireballs and lightning. No patience for a mending spell.
I practised my runes on the back of a bus ticket. They held for a whole stop.
The best spells are the ones nobody notices: a door that sticks less, a plant that perks up.
The Mages' Guild here wanted me to join. I said I would think about it, for a decade or two.
Magic in this world feels thinner, like air on a mountain.
My teacher said: a spell is a promise you keep with the world. I have kept mine, mostly.
I tried to charm the vending machine. It gave me two sodas. I paid for the second.
The gods here are at war with the mages. I keep my head down and my runes small.
A thousand years of study and still the hardest spell is getting seeds to sprout in a cold spring.
Magic and electricity are cousins, I think. They both hum when they are pleased.
I keep my grimorie wrapped in oilcloth. It is the only book I brought from home.
collective: I can hear the Naguka the way you hear rain on a roof. Constant, soft, sometimes a crash.
We learned to read their collective by magic. Only to read. Never to write.
I know that Naguka will knock over the table before he does. I move my tea anyway.
Somewhere a hundred Naguka just decided to {march|eat|shout} at once. I felt it like a draught.
The humans ask me to put a thought into the collective. I cannot. Nobody can, except the Junehem.
Harm one Naguka and the whole species knows. I see the news ripple through them before the papers do.
Reading the collective is like overhearing a very large, very loud family dinner.
The army asked me to spy for them through the collective. I told them I read; I do not report.
Knowing what comes next and being unable to change it. That is the Verden condition.
The collective dreams of caves, of a big drilled hole and of the light at the top of it.
Today the collective is calm. Somewhere, a great many Naguka are napping.
I closed my mind to the collective for a whole day. The silence was enormous.
Grissnack's voice runs through the collective like a crack through ice.
I can see the ambush coming. I cannot stop the Naguka from springing it. Only warn the others.
We see their next step, never their reasons. Often I suspect there are none.
naguka: The Naguka are our cousins in face only. Inside, they are human. Loud, warm, impatient humans.
They came up the Kola shaft in 1970 and have not stopped shouting since.
A Naguka asked me why I talk 'so many words'. I told him words are free. He took a great many.
I am very fond of the Naguka. From a reasonable distance.
The Naguka paint their faces for Junehem. I would rather they painted fences.
The Naguka children are delightful. They bite, but delightfully.
Humans mistake me for a Naguka, then I say a full sentence and they look relieved.
The Naguka never plant anything. They harvest everything. Usually other people's.
A Naguka gave me a dead rat as a gift. I thanked him properly. It is the thought.
I taught a Naguka to read three letters. He read them at everyone for a week.
The Naguka think we are very old, very slow cousins. They are half right.
Every Naguka is brave. Very few of them are careful. I would trade some of one for the other.
The Vatican wants to baptise the Naguka. The Naguka want to eat the incense.
They call me 'Blue Cousin'. It is the kindest thing a Naguka has ever called anyone.
A Naguka cannot wait for water to boil. I have seen one try to bite the kettle.
Goblin and human together make an orc. Goblin and Verden make nothing but conversation.
The Naguka are young as a people. Give them a few thousand years.
I knew that Naguka would fall in the fountain. I did not know he would enjoy it so much.
They speak like children, the humans say. Children who know a great many swear words.
Under all the noise, the Naguka are lonely for something. I think it is the dark under the earth.
integration: I filled in my seventh form this month. The humans love forms nearly as much as queues.
MarkovSpeak is a fine tongue. I speak it better than some of my neighbours, I am told.
I have a job, a flat, a library card and a favourite bench. I am integrated.
The Verden council meets the mayor next week about the community gardens. Fingers crossed.
My employer forgot I was a Verden until I brought in a pod for the office party.
Some humans call us 'the polite goblins'. There are worse names.
I pay my taxes. Nothing in the Fields prepared me for taxes.
My human neighbours invited me for {Christmas|a wedding|a birthday}. I brought a potted lemon tree.
I voted for the first time. I read every word on every poster first.
The young Verden here speak with human slang. Their elders pretend not to understand.
There is a Verden doctor at the clinic now. And a Verden teacher. One by one.
Integration is like grafting: done right, the join disappears in a few seasons.
I sometimes forget I am a refugee. Then the news mentions the Squishing.
The humans gave us a home without being asked twice. We should never forget it.
I am Verden at home and a citizen in the street. Some days the two get along.

positive: {b}! I brought you some tomatoes from the greenhouse. The first of the year.
For me? They smell amazing. Thank you, {a}.
Eat them slowly. They took four months.
My spore pod hummed this morning, {b}. For the first time.
Is that good? It sounds good.
It is the best news I have had since we left the Fields.
Then congratulations. Really.
You fixed my radio. I do not know how to thank you.
It was just a loose wire, {a}. Nothing special.
To you, a loose wire. To me, a miracle with an orchestra inside.
I passed my driving test, {b}. On the third attempt.
No way! How fast did you go?
Thirty kilometres an hour. The examiner said it was 'a new record for caution'.
Ha! Well, nobody's getting caught in a time loop at thirty.
You always say hello to me at the market. I want you to know it matters.
Of course I do. You're one of the nicest people round here, {a}.
Then we are both lucky.
*hands over a small potted plant* For your windowsill.
Oh, it's lovely! What is it?
A cutting from a Fields herb. It will outlive us both if you let it.
I foresaw that the Naguka would raid the bakery, so I warned the baker.
So that's why he closed early! You saved his week, {a}.
He gave me a whole loaf. I think I came out ahead.
I finally understand the bus timetable. All of it.
Then you understand more than most of us, {a}.
It only took me a year of patient study.
Can you teach me the Sunday one?
{b}, you look tired. Sit. I have made {tea|soup|honey bread}.
You're a lifesaver. It's been a long day.
Then let it be a short evening.
I read your grandmother's letter for you, as you asked. She is very proud of you.
She said that? Really?
Twice. Once in the middle and once at the end, underlined.
You lent me your umbrella last week. I have brought it back, dry and with a charm on it.
A charm? What does it do?
It will never turn inside out again. A small thing, but you will thank me in November.
The children at the school drew me. In every drawing I am smiling.
That's because you always are, {a}.
Not always. But around them, yes.
I won something at the arcade, {b}! A plastic dragon!
After how many tokens?
Do not ask. It is priceless.
*laughs* Fair enough.
Thank you for standing up for me on the tram yesterday.
That man was out of line. You've every right to be here.
Hearing that from you means more than any stamped paper.
Your garden is doing beautifully, {b}. The beans have doubled.
That's all your advice, {a}. I just did what you said.
Then you listened. That is the hardest part of gardening.
I finished the book you gave me. The one about the railways.
And? Did you like it?
I read it twice and then I went to the station just to look at a locomotive.
Ha, I knew you'd love it.
You remembered my name, {b}. Most people only remember the colour.
Well, you're {a}. Hard to forget.
Then I shall remember yours just as carefully.
Deal.
I was homesick all morning. Then you waved at me from across the street.
Just a wave, {a}.
Just a wave. Just the right one.
My cousin Naguka finally said 'please'. I have waited three years for this.
What did he want?
My sandwich. He got it, too. One must reward progress.
You helped me carry the seedlings home. All forty trays.
My arms are still complaining, {a}.
In a month I will repay them with salad.
I can read the collective, but I never foresaw a friend like you, {b}.
Well, I'm not a goblin. You'd need a different spell for me.
Then I am glad of the surprise.
The council approved the community garden, {b}! Thanks to your signatures.
I just knocked on a few doors.
Sixty doors. I counted. There will be a bed with your name on it.
Then I'd better learn to weed.
negative: You stepped on my seedlings again, {b}.
They're in the middle of the path! What do you expect?
I expect eyes to be used for looking.
Your radio is very loud at night.
And your greenhouse lamp shines right into my bedroom.
The plants need it. Do you need the football results at two in the morning?
Actually, yes.
You told the landlord I keep 'some kind of egg' in the cupboard.
Well, you do! It's weird, {a}.
It is my family. I would not call your children weird.
My children don't glow in the dark.
I knew you would be late. I did not need to read any collective for that.
The bus broke down! It's not my fault.
It never is, {b}. That is the remarkable thing.
You called me 'goblin' in front of your friends. In that tone.
You ARE a goblin. I don't see the problem.
The word is not the problem. The tone is.
{b}, you have been leaving your rubbish by my compost.
Compost is rubbish, isn't it?
Compost is a slow miracle. Your crisp packets are not.
You sold me a broken cassette player.
It worked when I sold it, {a}.
It worked for one song. I am patient, not foolish.
Fine. Fine! I'll give you five euros back.
Must you play Junehem in the courtyard, {b}?
It's music. You don't own the courtyard.
Neither do the Junehem, though they seem to think they own a great deal.
You took the last seat on the tram from an old woman.
I didn't see her, all right?
She stood right beside you for six stops.
I lent you my book in spring. It is autumn now.
I'm still reading it! You're the one always saying 'patience'.
Patience is for seeds, {b}, not for borrowers.
You told everyone at work that I can read minds.
Can't you?
Only goblin minds. And only the collective. Now the manager asks me who stole his stapler.
Did you tell him?
It was you, {b}. I did not need magic.
You cut down the hedge without asking.
It was blocking my parking space!
It was blocking it for forty years. Your car has been there for three weeks.
You threw away the seeds I saved for you, {b}.
They looked like little bits of dirt, {a}.
They were next year's garden. Now they are next year's nothing.
You laughed when I asked how the lift works.
Come on, it was funny. Everybody knows how a lift works.
Everybody here. I have known lifts for two years. You have known moss for none.
Your dog dug up my bulbs, {b}.
He's a dog. Dogs dig.
And owners apologise. That is how it works where I come from.
You keep telling people the Squishing is a hoax.
It's exaggerated. The news loves a scare.
My home is gone, {b}. Folded like a letter. Tell me again it is exaggerated.
I asked you to water the pod while I was away. One thing.
I forgot! Is it all right?
It will live. It is sulking, and so am I.
You let the Naguka kids into my greenhouse.
They were cold, {a}! What was I meant to do?
Give them a blanket. Not my melons.
...They did seem to enjoy the melons.
You owe me twenty euros, {b}. Since the summer.
I'll pay you back, I promise.
Promises grow on the same tree as excuses, in my experience.
neutral: Excuse me. Does this tram go to the station?
Number four does. This is the six.
Ah. Then I shall admire the six and wait for the four.
The weather has been unsettled lately.
Tell me about it. Rain one minute, sun the next.
Good for the gardens, at least.
Forgive me, is that a cassette player?
Yeah. Want to have a listen?
*listens* Extraordinary. The whole band, in your pocket.
It's just a cheap one, really.
Do you know where I can buy good compost around here?
Garden centre, past the bridge. Closes at six.
Thank you. I will walk slowly and still arrive in time.
Is this seat taken?
No, go ahead.
Thank you. My feet have been arguing with these shoes all day.
The bakery has a new loaf today. Rye and seeds.
Any good?
I bought two. That is my review.
You are reading about trains. May I ask which ones?
Old steam engines. My grandfather drove one.
A driver of a moving house. What a family to come from.
Did you hear the sirens last night, {b}?
Some trouble on the north side, I think.
I hope everyone is home safe.
The prices at the market have gone up again.
Everything's going up. Except wages.
Then I shall grow more and buy less.
Pardon me, how do I make this machine give me a ticket?
Press the green button, then put the coins in.
*presses* Oh! It printed. It printed for me.
Yeah... they do that.
The sky flickered over the river this morning. Did you see?
I did. Gave me the creeps.
It gives me the creeps too, and I have seen worse.
Your roses are lovely. Do you feed them?
Coffee grounds and banana peel, mostly.
A wise gardener. I shall try the banana.
What time does the library close today?
Seven, I think. Earlier on Saturdays.
Then I have two hours. Enough for one good chapter and one bad nap.
Have you lived on this street long?
A few years now. You?
Since the spring. The street is still deciding what it thinks of me.
It'll come round. Streets always do.
Like hedges. Give them time and they close the gap.
There is a Naguka asleep on the bench by the fountain.
Should we call someone?
No. He will wake in ten minutes and steal a pigeon. Then he will leave.
I have been told the post office is the place for stamps.
That's right. Or the tobacconist.
Two places for stamps. This world is generous.
The new shopping centre has stairs that move.
Escalators. They've been around for ages.
Not around me. I rode up and down four times.
Is it true there are monsters on the east road?
So people say. I'd take the bus.
Wise advice. I like the bus anyway.
I planted mint in the pot by the door. I hope nobody minds.
Mint spreads like crazy, you know.
I know. I am counting on it.
Do you know a good place to have a radio repaired?
There's a man on Via Roma. Old, slow, but good.
Old, slow and good. My kind of craftsman.
The election posters are everywhere, {b}.
Yeah. Same promises as last time.
Then I shall read them as I read old seed catalogues: hopefully, but with care.
How long have you worked in this shop?
Twelve years. Feels like a hundred some days.
Twelve years is a young tree. Plenty of growing left.
The river is high this week.
All that rain up in the hills.
The water remembers every drop. So do the banks.
May I ask what that song on your radio is?
Some pop thing. Charts this week.
It is very cheerful. I will forget it by tonight, but cheerfully.
The children are building something in the empty lot.
A fort, I think. Out of pallets.
A fine start. Next year, perhaps, a garden beside it.
Is the bank open on Saturdays here?
Mornings only.
Then the euros and I will wait until Monday.
You look lost, {b}. Can I help?
I'm looking for the clinic.
Two streets on, left at the bakery. Follow the smell of bread, then the smell of disinfectant.
The streetlights went out on our road last night.
Again? Someone should call the council.
I did. They said 'soon'. I have learned that 'soon' is a human season.
Do you play chess?
Badly. Why?
So do I. We would be perfectly matched.
There's been talk of the Horde moving south again.
There's always talk. Nothing ever happens here.
Let us hope this town stays dull, then.
What is that machine in the corner of the café?
A jukebox. You put in a coin and pick a song.
A coin for a song. I may never leave.
The swallows left early this year.
Cold winter coming, my mum always said.
Your mother read the birds. A useful skill.
How do you get a bicycle to stay upright?
You just keep pedalling.
Then it is like most things.
I saw a poster for a Junehem concert on the wall by the station.
Here? Who'd go to that?
Every Naguka within a hundred kilometres. I would stay indoors that night.
The pharmacy on the corner has closed.
Really? Where am I meant to go now?
There is another by the market. Smaller, but the pharmacist is patient.
Do you grow anything at home, {b}?
Just a cactus. I keep forgetting to water it.
Then you have chosen the right friend.
I heard the trains will be on strike tomorrow.
Great. Another day of buses.
I will miss the trains. I hope the drivers get what they ask for.
What is the name of that tree, the one with the white flowers?
A hawthorn, I think. Or a cherry. No idea, honestly.
A hawthorn. I asked to see if you knew. Forgive me, it is a gardener's game.
The town fair is next week, they say.
Oh, it's great. Food stalls, games, a band.
I will bring jam to sell. And go home with three cakes.

lines: I think my ancestors were wrong to throw their machines into the sun.
Maybe they knew something you don't. Look what machines have done here.
Here machines bring music, light and warm water. I see no ruin in a kettle.
Give it a few hundred years. Then ask again.
Magic is the better path. It asks patience, and patience makes good people.
Magic is for the few. A light switch works for everybody.
Anyone can learn a spell, given years.
Most people don't have years, {a}. They have a Tuesday.
The Horde will settle one day. They are young, not wicked.
They burned three villages last spring. Tell those people they're just young.
I do not excuse it. I only say they can change.
Then let them change somewhere far from here.
The Junehem are not gods. They are four men with very loud guitars.
Try telling that to the armies who couldn't kill them.
Belief keeps them alive. That makes them fed, not divine.
Sounds like a god to me.
The Squishing is the greatest danger any of us faces.
More than the Horde? More than the wars?
Wars end. The Squishing only grows.
...Yeah. When you put it like that, you're right.
Humans rush through everything. They taste nothing.

Knowing the future is a burden, not a gift.
